# Should you be in a relationship at all?

This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on. You’re not ready.

Some people would say that a good relationship can teach you self-love. True. The problem is that you need a good relationship at exactly the time you may be least capable of creating one, recognizing one, or keeping one good. The odds are terrible.

At twenty, I thought I was totally fine until I became enamored with Alba. She was Dominican, and warm in a way I didn’t understand. Kissing your BFF was normal to her. I thought she was in love with me. She did love me and wanted me living with her, but not in the way I wanted. The confusion threw me into a horrible spell for years. I was even a bit suicidal while living with her.

Then Bee cracked me open. My second wife and I were about as in love as two people could be, considering that every other day she would demonize me because of BPD. Before Bee, I didn’t know what In Love meant. Nobody knows until it happens. It’s a completely different kind of reality. It’s spiritual.

Did it heal her? We still can’t understand. During our two years together, it seemed to stabilize and heal some things while provoking her demons even more. Did it heal me? The relationship almost killed me, and I would never undo it. I still love her so much. I haven’t spoken with her in a year, but I love sending her love.

Relationships ALWAYS reveal what I can’t see. My selfishness. The depth that is actually available versus the depth I idealize. The other person’s selfishness and dishonesty and superficiality. How deeply I really love. How deep my illusions go. Whether my spirituality survives contact with another human being. Everything.

I’ve used spirituality as a replacement for intimacy a lot because intimacy was simply unavailable. As a boy and young man, I was so deprived of female touch that it was driving me insane. Meditation sometimes made the deprivation easier. The deprivation stayed.

Most people can’t be happy celibate. Distracted-happy, sure. Truly happy, I don’t believe it. Most people are not so serious about spiritual liberation that giving up sex and partnership for life makes sense. The Buddha didn’t advise most people to become monks.

Maybe you genuinely become happier and more peaceful as a monk or nun. Great. Stay. It might work for some very advanced people, or if your sexual desire is already low, or you’re old, etc.

The hard part is that lack of awareness is an epistemic problem. How do you know what you’re not aware of? Inner-child reparenting can help a lot, because often the inner child is being ignored while the adult is feeling some kind of liberation.

And if you’re so happy and free, what happens when you’re alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you? Or vice versa for women. Do you feel like you’re losing some control? Are you afraid?

Bhante Gunaratana tells a story like this in his autobiography. A super beautiful girl at a retreat he was teaching snuck into his room and waited for him naked. He went nuts and started screaming at her to get out at the top of his lungs. Obviously he was still repressing something, and she was adept at uncovering it (surely not her intent).

Robes do nothing. I was mildly molested in public by the abbot of one of Thailand’s largest Buddhist retreat centers. In Thailand, parents have very good reasons not to leave children alone with monks. Tibet is worse.

Forced celibacy doesn’t abolish anyone’s sexuality. For most people it eventually sends it somewhere weird. Why wouldn’t it?

And monasticism is not only about liberation. In a poor country, the robe can mean free food and somewhere to live, and you get to escape a lot of ordinary responsibilities. In the West the free food probably matters less. But somebody who got no particular respect as a layman can become Venerable Somebody and suddenly people are bowing to him.

Maybe he sincerely wants liberation too. Sure. Why wouldn’t he? People can want several things at once.

Then there are practical partnerships.

I travel the world as a (white) guy from a first-world country. Many women have wanted to marry me partly because they figured I could improve their status and comfort. That always makes me feel sad and lonely to think about, but yeah, I know it's to be expected.

It’s reasonable for a woman to want support, since after all she has to provide for her potential children, but it muddies the waters for me. I'm not stupid, I understand that she might really love me while still wanting money, stability, children, a visa, a home, etc. Men aren't a different species, although sometimes I think I might be. A man can really love a woman for who she is while also seeing her as a source of sex, children, social legitimacy, or help running the house. Affection and practical motives often coexist, even if it isn't the romantic ideal.

And hey, sometimes being objectified is kinda sexy, too. Men like to be objectified to a certain degree as providers and defenders, just as women often like being seen as sex dolls by the men they want. Being wanted that way feels good, but feeling held is important as well.

I don’t want to be just a provider-and-defender machine, because that's vulnerable to hypergamy. I wanna know that if I fall ill or lose my job, I can count on my wife still. Guys want a ride-or-die chick. A woman also wants to know that when she gets old, sick, or no longer looks like the fantasy that first attracted her man, he will still happily stay.

But beyond all that practical stuff, sex is extremely important for building and renewing the connection. I have also said that if two people aren't having sex, it becomes hard to explain how they're different from regular friends. The apparent contradiction is mostly a matter of timing.

I think sex is especially important while the bond is forming. It may be what turns a friendship into a romance and keeps feeding the romantic connection. But if the connection gets deep enough, sex appeal stops being the basis of the relationship. You don’t stop loving the person because she got old, he lost his job, one of you got sick, or sex became impossible.

Sometimes they may even want you to find sexual satisfaction elsewhere if they can’t give it, because they love you and want you to be happy. Maybe they don’t. Nobody is owed that as proof of love.

Partnership is generally healthier for people who are ready for it. A good community is generally healthier than isolated living. Celibacy may be right for some people. I can’t tell any particular person which life is morally superior.

I would still advise most of my friends not to date yet. They have too many problems. Then again, they are lonely, and loneliness kills. That is the catch-22.

## How to find a partner

Looking for a partner is arguably backward, and can work against you. You can’t help looking if you want one, but once you start seeing every new person as a potential partner, you perform for them and they perform for you. Try to see people for who they are before you think of them that way. Actually it was Bee who kept drilling this into me: "You see a pretty girl, but you don't see the ugly stuff she's dealing with inside."

On the other hand, if you aren't looking for one, then you also aren't filtering & comparing potential matches, which makes you more vulnerable to someone who targets you with their love bombs.

Maybe a good compromise is to look for people that match you without directly looking for a romantic match. Join a local group that fits your interests. Go forage for wild plants, meditate, hike, study philosophy, whatever. At least you have fun, learn something, and maybe make some friends even if nobody attractive shows up.

I would never recommend dating apps based on my own experience, although I suppose it depends on the person. Maybe you don’t care much about spirituality or anything, you’re not unique and don’t care if they are, you just "like big butts and you cannot lie," and they want the same sort of thing. Then maybe the app fits what you're looking for. 😅

Case in point, OKCupid didn't tell me my first wife was going to try to kill me and my family, take my son, and then put me on child support that I can't pay and wouldn't pay on principle if I could. That was the worst choice I ever made.

On the other hand, the app did give me information that I ignored because she was cute and interested in me. Her OKCupid profile almost made her sound like a prostitute, or at least someone who liked casual sex. Both turned out to be true. But once she started chatting with me and I saw the nice photos, I thought maybe she had been joking in the profile or something.

These days almost nobody even has a profile. They just have photos, which is showing you something too.

Ok wait, Judge not, lest ye be judged... An app could be fine as an introduction if you use it as a proper gate. Assume 99.99% of the people there are a bad match for you. If you’re just going to get excited by every cute guy or girl who hits you up, forget it. That’s such an easy way to find a weirdo, a psycho, a mooch, a faker, or whatever. Those people are easy enough to find in modern society in person anyway.

I always tell young guys especially: don’t worry about not finding a girl. Worry about finding the wrong girl. Girls are usually more selective, but they still need to think twice, because they often go for guys who aren’t respectful or mature.

I recently tried Hinge again for a few days while I was in Kenya after my last breakup. I was getting something like a hundred girls interested in my profile every day, so I looked through a lot of profiles. Some were cute but none seemed deep. So the app did tell me something useful.

Sometimes when you don't go looking, others go looking for you! My dad at one point decided I needed a girlfriend. This was long before dating apps, so he suggested we put up posters around the neighborhood advertising me as eligible for girls to date. I was horrified and we dropped the idea. That gives you some idea of the mildly autistic background I’m coming from: we didn’t understand people. That's why it might seem absurd the level to which I'm trying here to help you understand what perhaps is already obvious. 😅

The advantage of meeting through your community, unlike through an app, is that you see someone over time. Other people know them. You see how they act when they aren’t on a date, what they’re like with friends, and what happens when they’re irritated, bored, jealous, or not getting what they want.

Community also supports you regardless of who your baby daddy may be, and you aren’t desperate for just any kind of closeness because hopefully the community already fulfills most of that need.

But if you don't have community, the move is to find someone who is also looking for one that would interest you both. You can visit communities together, or at least make a real plan to eventually live in one together. It’s a wide world, and traveling around looking at possible communities is a supremely good way to get to know someone.

On the other hand, you may end up having sex too fast if you’re traveling together, but I'd still rather have sex with someone who's trying to find a commune with me than someone I met at a party.

# Starting on the right foot

## The window of clarity, and how it closes

For me, the window of objectivity starts closing abruptly once it seems like sex will definitely be happening soon and I’m flowing with that timeline. I begin idealizing her more, and after sex I may suddenly feel unable to leave because maybe she’s pregnant, etc.

Maybe I’m not representative of the modern degen dating scene. If you’re quite numb and used to casual sex, perhaps the window closes later, or even never. But for me, this is the pattern, and it seems like it would be healthy in a healthy, natural, small society.

The attachment theory part isn’t just from my own experience. It comes from reading I’ve done as well. Sex turns on bonding chemistry—oxytocin, dopamine, vasopressin—that usually biases us toward attachment. People call oxytocin the “love hormone,” as if getting more attached should make you feel closer and safer. If closeness was safe when you were little, maybe it does feel a bit like coming home. But if it came with neglect, abuse, or if people disappeared on you, you can get more attached and more freaked out at the same time. You might get anxious or suspicious. You might feel worthless or fight or flight mode may kick in.

Before the wisdom window closes, the main thing is to find out whether you are actually compatible. Do you have the same goals and values, especially around children, health, love, and romance? Where do you want to live? Do you both want to find a community? What kind of relationship do you want with technology and money?

Ask deep questions. Conversation-card games may seem silly, but they can help people get past superficial talk and see if they’re compatible.

But asking, “How do you handle jealousy?” can get me a beautiful answer that tells me almost nothing. I’d rather ask what she thinks she would do in an actual situation. If all she can give me is a general answer, I assume she probably doesn't know yet.

I can learn a lot by talking, but there's a point where more questions mostly teach me what the person says about themself. After that I need ordinary time. Ten profound conversations in one weekend may tell me we can have profound conversations. They don't tell me what she's like on a boring day, or when she's annoyed and doesn't have an answer prepared.

You can also bring the person to a party and see how they act, bring them around your family or friends, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too. Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see how it feels. Is it weird? Are they wondering why you do this stuff? Do they look bored, like they’d rather just hit you up later than be with you while you’re doing ordinary stuff? Can you guys be normal together and not just romantic or dating?

See their negative side first too. If there is no negative side, that’s a red flag for fakery. Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient afternoon. How recent is the healing story—two months or two years? Jealousy, abandonment, possessiveness, and the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story may not show up until there is stress and entanglement. By then, of course, you’re stressed and entangled.

Sometimes the only thing I have is a little “wait” feeling. It doesn't prove anything. But if I'm about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that's enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.

If they’re nasty to their friends, family, or other people, assume they will eventually be nasty to you. We mostly seem to get attracted to the inner-child part because we’re coming from our inner child and we want to have fun. But you also need to find out whether there is a healthy adult there before you’re too bonded to want the answer.

## Things get tricky fast

Couples withdraw from friends who aren’t supportive of the romantic dyad, and they also stop telling friends the truth. Friends hear less. Sharp questions start to feel rude. An obvious problem dissolves into, "but I love her," and the small world of the relationship starts feeling more real than the rest of life.

Sometimes withdrawing isn’t wrong. Telling your friend, “Can you believe what my girlfriend is doing to me?” can be a privacy violation. It’s just important to realize what is happening.

The relationship can close off at exactly the point when both people most need a view from outside it.

## Anti-PTSD Can Be Just As Dangerous As PTSD

When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.

A friend of mine was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good. I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD.

My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

That dynamic alone isn’t necessarily the main problem. A lot of women have seen me that way. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something deeply traumatic—like they’re acting out a taboo fantasy, or they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child. She would tell you the same.

She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, she said the magic words: “I would rather be with you in the forest than with any other man in a mansion.”

Best drug I ever had.

I don’t know whether it ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.

So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up doesn’t want her dad in the same way. That wasn’t the whole story. The two years in between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes. We barely made it through.

Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, [I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/i-ate-loveyhuasca-every-day-for-90), and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.

That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

## Beware idealization in either direction

Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural protector/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.

It shouldn’t have to happen that way, though. It’s a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. Once you start identifying with the way you see them—she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her—you’re already lost in the sauce.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me. I don’t mean this as a clinical diagnosis, but I use it almost diagnostically in my own life. If a woman says, “He’s such a great guy. Of course he has flaws like anyone, but I love him,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “He’s perfect. I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the splitting happens, private hatred can replace worship. Then come public accusations, rewriting the whole past and treating every flaw as proof that the person was fake all along. Sometimes the woman who thought I was perfect later accuses me of thinking I’m perfect.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine.

Seeing someone’s highest potential is different from ignoring what is actually there. You can see something in a person before she fully lives it, but then you have to ask her:

“I see this in you, and I think it’s special. Do you wanna reach for it together?”

If she says no, forget it. You’re in la la land. If she says yes, ask what is blocking her. Is the block more than you can handle? Or does she mostly need somebody to join her on the journey and believe in her?

Partners should help each other grow. Who else is going to do it? Your mom and dad? You’re already grown. Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you’d better choose someone who helps you grow well. Like the FM Laeti song here says, “Inspire her to see the best in herself, actualize that.” If something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.

So hold your horses a bit more than you’d like to. See if your partner still praises you after a cold feud.

Ask what flaws she sees in you from time to time. Notice whether either of you is relating to a real human being or just to the divine archetypal energy the other person temporarily opened.

I’ve been through the wringer so much with idealization that now no matter who praises me I’m basically like, “Okay, thanks.” I try to do my best.
